nameStory: Purple willow gets its name from the purplish-red color of its young twigs and branches, especially noticeable in winter and early spring. When the bark catches the light, it shows off beautiful reddish-purple hues that make this willow stand out from its green-barked cousins.
description: Purple willow is a graceful shrub or small tree that typically grows 6-15 feet tall, though it can reach up to 20 feet in ideal conditions. It has a rounded, bushy shape with multiple stems arising from the base, creating an attractive fountain-like form. The narrow, bluish-green leaves give it a delicate appearance, and like all willows, it loves wet places. Originally from Europe and Asia, it's been planted widely in New England gardens and has naturalized in some wetland areas.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young twigs and branches display distinctive purplish-red to reddish-brown bark that's smooth to the touch and particularly vibrant in winter sunlight - this is the plant's signature feature

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves are 2-4 inches long with a distinctive blue-green or grayish-green color above and pale underneath, feeling smooth and somewhat thick when rubbed between fingers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, fuzzy catkins appear in early spring before the leaves emerge - male catkins are silvery-gray and female catkins are greenish, both about 1-2 inches long

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a multi-stemmed shrub or small tree with gracefully arching branches that often bend toward the ground, creating an elegant, fountain-like silhouette

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Winter buds are small, pointed, and pressed tightly against the purplish twigs, covered with a single scale that feels smooth when touched

habitat: Purple willow thrives in moist to wet soils near streams, pond edges, wetlands, and low-lying areas that stay damp. In New England, you'll often find it in gardens and landscaped areas, especially around water features, but it has also naturalized in some wetland margins and floodplains. It tolerates a wide range of soil types as long as they don't dry out completely.

seasonality.spring: Silvery catkins emerge before the leaves in March or April, followed by the distinctive blue-green foliage. The purple bark color is still quite prominent and makes identification easy.
seasonality.summer: Full leafy canopy of narrow, blue-green leaves creates a soft, feathery texture. The purple bark coloring may be less noticeable under the full foliage but is still visible on newer growth.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow before dropping, and the purple-red bark becomes more visible again as the plant goes dormant. Fall color is not particularly showy compared to other trees.
seasonality.winter: This is when purple willow is most distinctive - the bare purple-red twigs and branches stand out beautifully against snow and gray winter landscapes, making it easy to spot and identify.

funFact: Purple willow's flexible, strong branches have been prized by basket makers for centuries - it's considered one of the finest basket-weaving willows in the world, with some European basketry traditions dating back over 2,000 years still using this exact species today!
confusionNotes: Purple willow can be confused with other willows, but the purple-red bark color is usually distinctive. If the bark isn't clearly purple, look for the blue-green leaf color - most other willows have brighter green leaves. Remember: "Purple bark, blue leaves" to distinguish it from green-barked willows with regular green foliage.
contextualKnowledge: Purple willow is sometimes called "basket willow" in gardening contexts, which can be confusing since there's also a separate species specifically called basket willow (Salix viminalis). Many purple willows sold in nurseries are actually cultivated varieties selected for especially vibrant bark color, so garden specimens may look more purple than wild ones.
compareHints: Among New England's willows, purple willow is unique for its purple-red bark and blue-green leaves - pussy willow has gray bark and broader leaves, while black willow has dark, furrowed bark. White willow also has grayish leaves but grows much larger and has silvery-white bark, not purple-red bark like purple willow.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many willow species, pussy willow stands out for its exceptionally soft, silvery catkins that appear before the leaves.
Bearberry willow is instantly distinguished from all other New England willows by its unique prostrate growth - every other willow species grows upright as shrubs or trees.
Among New England's willows, heart-leaved willow stands out for its combination of thick, persistently fuzzy-bottomed leaves with heart-shaped bases.
Among New England's willows, Bebb's willow stands out for its dense thicket-forming habit and adaptability to various soil types.

Among New England willows, rusty willow is most similar to grey willow (Salix cinerea), but rusty willow's twigs have that distinctive reddish-brown coloration versus grey willow's more grayish twigs.
Among New England's many willow species, black willow stands out as the largest tree form with the darkest bark.
Among New England willows, prairie willow is unique in preferring dry, sunny sites while most others need moist to wet conditions.
Grey willow differs from native pussy willow by having much more pronounced silvery-gray, woolly leaf undersides and tends to form denser thickets.
Among New England's many willows, silky willow stands out for its distinctly silky leaf undersides - most other willows have smooth or only lightly hairy leaf backs.
Interior sandbar willow stands out from other New England willows by having the narrowest leaves in the genus - much thinner than pussy willow's oval leaves or black willow's lance-shaped ones.
Meadow willow is much shorter and more colony-forming than most other New England willows like black willow or pussy willow.
Among New England's willows, shining willow stands out for its exceptional height and mirror-like leaves.

Unlike the familiar pussy willow with its large, fuzzy catkins and broad leaves, or the water-loving black willow with its narrow leaves, tea-leafed willow has those distinctive thick, oval leaves with prominent parallel veining.
Among New England willows, sage-leaf willow is unique for its distinctly fuzzy, silvery leaves that truly resemble herb sage.
Among New England's many willows, balsam willow is unique for its strong balsam fragrance - most other willows are essentially scentless.
Among New England willows, least willow is unmistakable due to its ground-hugging growth - all other willows in our region grow as upright shrubs or trees.
Bog willow differs from its willow relatives by staying much shorter and preferring acidic bog conditions rather than streamside locations.
Among New England's many willows, satiny willow stands out for having the most dramatically silvery leaf undersides—much more pronounced than the similar silky willow or sage-leaf willow.
Among New England's willows, white willow stands out for its especially silvery leaf undersides and larger mature size.
Unlike the familiar pussy willow with its large, showy catkins and bigger leaves, or the tall black willow found along rivers, Labrador willow stays remarkably small and compact.
Unlike native New England willows such as pussy willow or black willow, dappled willow has variegated foliage and often opposite leaves rather than alternate ones.

Among New England willows, autumn willow stands out for its completely hairless leaves and stems - unlike pussy willow's fuzzy twigs, silky willow's silky leaf undersides, or meadow willow's slightly hairy stems.
Among New England's willows, blueleaf willow is distinguished by its blue-green foliage color - most other willows have bright green or silvery leaves.
Unlike other New England willows such as pussy willow or black willow that have upright or spreading branches, weeping willow is unmistakable due to its pendulous, drooping branch structure.
Among New England's willows, peachleaf willow stands out for its impressive tree size - most of our native willows like pussy willow or silky willow are shrubs or small trees.
Unlike most New England willows which have narrow, lance-shaped leaves, goat willow stands out with its broad, oval, wrinkled leaves that look more like those of a poplar or apple tree.

Basket willow stands out among New England's willows for its extremely narrow leaves and exceptionally long, straight, flexible branches - most native willows like pussy willow or black willow have broader leaves and shorter, less flexible shoots.
Among New England's many willow species, rose-gold pussy willow stands out for its ornamental catkin colors - most native willows like common pussy willow have plain silver-gray catkins.
